scope: Personal-finance angle only: what an ETF is (the tradable basket), how its shares are bought and sold, the exchange-traded versus end-of-day pricing distinction from mutual funds, headline benefits with one line each, the honest market-risk note, and the one-line fact that many ETFs track an index. Fund-structure theory belongs to the finance subject; mutual funds, stocks, bonds, investing, and diversification are sibling topics referenced by name only, with their depth left to their own lessons.

claims.claim: An ETF is a pooled investment that trades on exchanges like a stock: it pools money from many investors and invests it in stocks, bonds, or other securities, and each share represents part ownership of the fund's portfolio — the working definition attributed to SEC Investor.gov.
ETF shares are bought and sold on national stock exchanges at market prices during trading hours, and retail investors typically need a brokerage account to trade them.

The key distinction from mutual funds is pricing and trading: mutual fund shares are bought from and sold back to the fund at the net asset value calculated at the end of each business day, while ETF shares trade on an exchange at market prices throughout the trading day.

Headline benefits of ETFs are diversification (many invest in a range of companies and industries, lowering the impact of one company's failure), low costs (typically lower expense ratios than comparable mutual funds), and tradability (buying and selling at market prices whenever the market is open).

ETFs carry market risk like any investment: they are not guaranteed or insured by the FDIC or any other government agency, and investors may lose some or all of their money if the securities held by the fund fall in value.
Many ETFs track an index: index funds follow a passive strategy designed to achieve approximately the same return as a particular index before fees.
Some ETFs are less diverse than others — they may hold few investments or even track a single stock — so the ETF label describes how the product trades, not how diversified it is.

conflictingEvidence: No material conflicts found among the sources. CFI states that ETFs 'typically have significantly lower expense ratios than a comparable mutual fund' — a general tendency, matching Investor.gov's note that fees and expenses vary from fund to fund. The lesson therefore presents low costs as a typical benefit, not a universal promise. Investor.gov and CFI agree on intraday trading and end-of-day mutual fund pricing.

sourceRecords.title: Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator). Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition (an ETF is an exchange-traded investment product that pools money from many investors and invests in stocks, bonds, or other securities; each share represents part ownership of the fund's portfolio); buying and selling ETF shares on national stock exchanges at market prices through a brokerage account; benefits (professional management, diversification across companies and industries, low minimum investment, liquidity at market prices whenever the market is open, tax advantage); the honest risk note (like mutual funds, ETFs are not guaranteed or insured by the FDIC or any other government agency, and investors may lose some or all of their money if the securities in the fund fall in value); index funds as a passive strategy aiming to match a particular index before fees; the warning that some ETFs are less diverse than others and may track a single stock. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Characteristics of Mutual Funds and Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) – Investor Bulletin
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A Investor Bulletin dated April 29, 2025. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports: both fund types pool investor money and each share represents proportionate ownership of the portfolio; the pricing distinction (mutual fund shares are bought and sold at the net asset value, typically calculated at the end of each business day; ETF shares are bought and sold on a national stock exchange at the prevailing market price throughout the trading day); mutual fund shares are bought from and sold back to the fund while retail investors buy and sell ETF shares only in market transactions and need a brokerage account; diversification applies to both types and helps lower risk if one company fails, with some funds less diverse than others; passive-strategy funds are typically called index funds; investors in both types pay fees and expenses. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Exchange Traded Fund (ETF)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B concept explainer. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Corroborates: an ETF is an investment fund holding a portfolio of assets that is traded like a stock throughout the trading day at fluctuating prices; many ETFs track indexes; ETFs typically have significantly lower expense ratios than comparable mutual funds; ETFs are more liquid than mutual funds, which can only be bought or sold at their end-of-day closing price; ETFs still carry transaction costs such as bid-ask spreads and commissions. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.
